Q4016336.summary: A monumental wooden crucifix of the Lucca type: Christ stands alive on the cross as King and Priest, wearing a long, sleeved tunic bound with a golden band, a stole over his shoulders, his eyes open and his head slightly inclined. Like the Volto Santo of Lucca, it was popularly attributed to Nicodemus, and a legend held that its face, carved separately, reproduced the true face of Christ. Radiocarbon dating of the wood points to the 8th–9th century, while the painted surface revealed by the restoration of 1984–1989 dates from around 1200, making it one of the oldest monumental sculptures of the medieval West.
facts: The sculpture is the result of at least three campaigns: wood radiocarbon-dated to the 8th–9th century, a possible reworking in the 11th–12th century suggested by its style, polychromy of the late 12th or early 13th century, and a left arm replaced in the early 13th century.

It is documented in the parish church (pieve) of Santa Maria at Sansepolcro from 1336 and was moved to the cathedral in 1770; the local story that the Cattani family donated it in 1405 is therefore legendary.
Pope Benedict XVI paused in prayer before it on 13 May 2012, during the millennium of the city.
Q4016336.notes: Radiocarbon dating: it.wikipedia reports only '8th/9th century' for the wood (from the restoration published by A. M. Maetzke, 1994); a more precise range (e.g. late 8th–early 9th century) could not be verified. Dimensions from it.wikipedia (280 × 290 cm); Wikidata gives height 280 cm.

cur:manuscripts-prayer-book-charles-bald.summary: On a gold cross set against a deep blue ground, Christ hangs with arms stretched wide and head inclined, his body sturdy and modelled in pink, wearing a loincloth; above the titulus a hand of God emerges with a wreath, flanked by a star-like sun and the moon, and a serpent writhes at the foot of the cross. On the facing page the crowned king kneels in prayer before the crucified Christ.
facts: German Wikipedia describes this as the oldest surviving prayer book made for private use; it is tiny, about 14 by 11.5 cm, with 46 leaves written entirely in gold.
The double page fol. 38v–39r, placed before a prayer in veneration of the Holy Cross, holds the book's only figurative images: Charles the Bald kneeling and the crucified Christ.

cur:manuscripts-otto-iii-prayer-book-cru.summary: Against a red ground written over with a prayer in gold letters, Christ hangs on the cross with arms stretched wide, his head bowed, wearing a striped loincloth; the Virgin and John the Evangelist stand mourning on either side, and above the cross-arm two winged, haloed busts lament — identified in German Wikipedia as personifications of the Sun and Moon. The image opens the book, before the penitential psalms.
facts: Made between 984 and 991 for the private use of the young King Otto III, this is the only surviving prayer book of an Ottonian king; it is tiny (15 × 12 cm), written in gold on painted purple, with five full-page miniatures.
German Wikipedia describes this as the first miniature, facing a Deesis on the recto.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-56-christ.summary: On top of a hill the bearded, cross-nimbed Christ-Logos stands in a mandorla supported by two angels, surrounded by eleven men who may be the apostles: 'be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens'. Below, angels turn to face armed aggressors, and lions and men with spears and sharp swords threaten the psalmist, who stands with his harp: 'awake, psaltery and harp'. The balanced design is among the most monumental in the book.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-56-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-gandersheim-gospels-cover-as.summary: Within borders of inhabited vine scroll, the ivory shows Christ ascending in a mandorla, lifted by two angels toward the hand of God, while two further angels bow beneath and the Virgin and the apostles gather below, gazing upward. The ivory was later set in a silver-gilt frame. It belongs to the refined Metz school of Carolingian ivory carving.
facts: The Coburg collections describe it as the book cover of the Gandersheim Gospels, Metz ivory of about 860–870, with a silver-gilt frame added in 1555 (inv. Pl.001).

walters:71.297.summary: Carved from a tall curved section of tusk, this ivory shows the Virgin seated with the Christ Child on her lap; he throws his arm round her neck and presses his cheek to hers, while she gazes straight ahead with large, fixed eyes. At the right a standing attendant holds a staff, and a small face appears in the upper corner. The Walters calls it one of the earliest examples of the tender embrace later known in Byzantium as the Eleousa, or Virgin of Tenderness.
facts: The museum suggests the relief was an icon for private devotion, in a monastic or domestic setting, and singles out the large head, fixed gaze and angular drapery as typical of early medieval Christian Egypt.
It is unusually large for an ivory, about 26 cm high, its shape following the curve of the tusk.
It was in Cologne in the 1870s and passed through two Paris sales before Henry Walters bought it in 1905.
walters:71.297.notes: Date 7th–8th century per the Walters (Commons gives 7th century).
